PREFACE. 

First  Edition  1877. 


"  Few  families  in  the  country  have  been  more  celebrated 
than  the  Cushings,  and  probably  no  other  has  furnished 
more  Judges  for  our  Probate,  Municipal,  and  Supreme 
Courts.  In  all  its  branches  it  has  been  highly  respectable, 
and  it  still  maintains  its  ancient  standing," —  History  of 
Hanover,  Mass,  by  J.  S.  Barry,  Boston,  1853.  High 
praise,  but  by  no  means  undeserved,  as  the  merest  gla/hce 
down  the  "  bead  roll  of  fame,"  as  imperfectly  transcribed 
in  this  work,  will  convince  the  most  sceptical.  The 
Genealogy  of  the  Gushing  Family  forms  of  itself  almost  a 
synopsis  of  the  colonizing  and  early  settlement  of  the 
New  England  States  and  a  portion  at  least  of  the  Pro- 
vince of  Quebec,  and  by  that  best  and  purest  of  its  stock, 
the  Puritans,  Here  we  read,  as  in  a  history,  the  mode  of 
settlement ;  the  organization  of  local  and  general  offices 
for  the  proper  and  regular  administration,  civil  and 
military,  of  the  affairs  of  the  colonies  ;  the  origin  of  the 
causes  which  led  to  the  memorable  struggle  for  Indepen- 
dence of  the  British  Colonies  in  America  ;  the  difficulties 
to  be  contended  with  in  the  re-organization  of  the  affairs 
of  the  young  nation,  its  laws  and  government.  In  the 
halls  of  the  Legislature,  in  the  administration  of  the  laws, 
in  the  arena  of  commerce  and  in  all  the  religious  contro- 
versies of  the  times  in  which  they  lived,  the  members  of 
this  remarkable  family  appear  almost  pre-eminent. 

The  scrupulous  accuracy  with  which  the  Pilgrim  P'athers 
recorded  the  births  and  marriages  of  the  colonists  makes 


4  PREFACE 

it  a  matter  of  no  great  difficulty  in  tracirg  the  descendants 
of  the  early  settlers  down  to  at  least  the  middle  of  the 
eighteenth  century  ;  and  from  the  exceptionally  prominent 
part  taken  in  all  public  matters  by  members  of  this  family, 
their  descent  can  be  traced  by  nearly  if  not  all  of  the  name 
to  the  present  day.  The  work  now  set  forth  is,  for  ought 
the  author  knows,  the  first  issued  with  any  pretensions  to 
a  general  genealogical  record.  It  is  necessarily  incom- 
plete  in  many  of  its  details,  and  many  precious  fragments 
remain  in  his  hand*;,  for  lack  of  the  necessary  links  to 
connect  them  with  the  rest  of  the  chain. 

LEMUEL  GUSHING. 
Present  Edition  1905. 

After  the  publication  of  the  first  edition  Mr.  Lemuel 
Gushing  collected  considerable  material,  intending  to  issue 
a  more  complete  record,  but  at  the  time  of  his  death,  in 
1881,  the  work  was  still  unfinished. 

In  190 1,  in  response  to  requests  from  various  members 
of  the  family,  it  was  decided  to  complete  the  task,  and 
the  present  volume  is  the  result  of  the  succeeding  four 
years'  work. 

While  much  additional  information  has  been  gathered 
and  the  history  of  the  family  greatly  extended,  it  must 
be  admitted  that  the  record  is  still  in  a  measure  incom- 
plete. This  is  due  paitly  to  the  fact  of  the  family  being 
now  scattered  all  over  the  United  States  and  Ganada, 
and  partly  because  the  work  had  to  be  done  almost 
altogether  by  correspondence,  the  writer  not  having  the 
necessary  time  and  means  to  personally  visit  the  various 
family  centres. 

The  scheme  adopted  is  that  which  is  in  use  by  the 
j^ew  England  Historical  and  Genealogical  Society.     The 


t>REPACE  .  5 

figure  which  precedes  the  name  of  the  head  of  a  family 
refers  back  to  the  family  of  the  immediate  ancestor,  where 
the  same  person  is  designated  in  the  li.>.t  of  children  by 
the  same  number  at  the  left  of  the  Romin  numeral.  The 
Christian  names  and  figures  which  are  given  in  par- 
enthesis after  the  head  of  a  family  denote  the  ancestral 
line  and  generation  in  consecutive  order. 

The  record  is  given  in  the  appendix  of  several  uncon- 
nected branches  of  the  family.  Most  of  these  are  of 
families  who  have  come  to  America  during  the  past 
century,  and  who,  while  not  immediately  connected  with 
the  great  American  branch,  doubtless  sprang  originally 
from  the  same  stock. 

Prior  to  1752  the  year  began  on  the  25th  of  March. 
In  this  year  a  change  was  m.ade  to  the  present  system  of 
reckoning  the  year  from  the  ist  of  January.  Conse- 
quently in  records  of  events  happening  prior  to  1752  the 
'Old  Style"  has  been  used  ;  in  the  present  volume  all 
dates  have  been  given  according  to  the  *'  New  Style,"  and 
changes  have  been  made  in  the  dates  taken  from  the 
records,  wherever  necessary  to  make  them  conform  to  the 
**  New  Style,"  e.  g.  the  date  of  Matthew  Cushing's  (No.  8) 
baptism  is  given  in  the  church  records  as  2  March,  1588, 
and  this  is  corrected  to  2  March,  1589. 

The  authorities  and  sources  of  information  utilized  in 
compiling  the  book  have  been  so  numerous  that  it  is  im- 
possible to  give  them  in  detail.  In  brief,  all  the  local 
histories  of  New  England  and  American  genealogies  in 
the  Boston  Public  Library,  the  Cambridge  Library,  and 
the  Library  of  the  New  England  Historical  and  Genealo- 
gical Society  of  Boston,  have  been  reviewed  and  most  of 
them   have  afforded  various   facts  and   details.     Special

mention  may,  however,be  made  of  the  Historyof  Hingham, 
1893,  the  Buckingham  Genealogy  1892  and  the  New 
England  Historical  and  Genealogical  Register.as  furnishing 
much  valuable  information.  Besides  these  sources  of  infor- 
mation the  town  and  church  records  of  Hingham,  Scituate, 
Rehoboth,  Pembroke,  Hull  and  many  other  places  were 
also  examined.  1  he  more  recent  history  of  the  family  has 
been  furnished  by  many  persons  in  the  United  States  and 
Canada.  As  members  of  nearly  all  the  branches  given  in 
this  book  have  contributed  information  in  regard  to  their 
own  line,  they  cannot  be  mentioned  by  name.  Among 
those  who  have  rendered  valuable  assistance  outside  of 
their  own  line,  the  special  thanks  of  the  author  are  due 
to  Mr.  Charles  C.  Gushing  (who  kindly  made  many  resear- 
ches in  the  Boston  Libraries),  Mrs.  David  Gushing  of 
Hingham,  Mass.,  Miss  J.  Mac  G.  Shaw  of  Boston,  Tappan

INTRODUCTION. 


The  Name  "  Cashing.'' 

The  derivation  of  the  name  is  somewhat  uncertain. 
The  present  form  is  used  by  all  the  American  descendants 
of  Matthew  Gushing  who  came  to  America  in  1638,  and 
was  probably  the  established  orthography  for  several 
generations  before  this,  as  the  English  and  Irish  branches 
use  the  same  spelling.  Bt-fore  the  sixteenth  century, 
however,  like  most  proper  names,  it  was  most  variously 
written.  For  example,  in  various  deeds,  wills  and  charters 
still  extant  in  Norfolk,  Eng.,  referring  to  the  direct  lineal 
ancestors  of  Matthew,  w^e  find  Cushyng,  Cushin,  Cushyn, 
Cusshyn,  Cussheyn,  Cusseyn,  Cussyn,  Cusyn,  and  Cosyn. 
Before  the  fourteenth  century  it  was  spelled  Cusyn,  Cosyn, 
or  Cosseyn  ;  after  this  it   is   always   spelt  with   a  //   and 


8  INTRODUCTION 

generally  sh,  e.g.,  Cussheyn,  Cusshyn.  The  final  g  does 
no-t  appear  until  1 500,  when  we  find  Cushy ng,  though 
Cushyn  and  Cushin  are  stiil  frequent  spellings. 

The  theories  advanced  by  certain  authorities  that  the 
name  is  a  corruption  of  MacOssian  or  MacAsswain,  or 
that  it  is  derived  from  the  word  '  Cush  '  with  the  suffix 
*ing'  (son  of)  may  be  mentioned  as  pure  guess-work, 
altogether  discredited  by  the  above  facts.  There  is  no 
evidence  that  the  name  is  Irish  as  some  have  asserted  ; 
the  Cushings  of  Ireland  appear  to  have  gone  there  in 
Cromwell's  time. 

The  late  Mr.  Frank  Hamilton  Cushirg,  to  whose 
researches  we  are  indebted  for  much  of  our  knowledge  of 
the  earlier  history  of  the  Cushings,  makes  two  sugges- 
tions: —  I  J/,  that  the  name  is  derived  from  the  Anglo- 
Norman  designation  of  Cousin  (Cosseyn  or  Cusseyn) ;  or, 
2;/<^, -that  it  arose  from  usage  in  connection  with  the  land 
title  of  Cossey.  Thus,  in  the  '  Domesday  '  of  William 
the  Conqueror,  we  find  that  "  the  ancient  village  and 
manor  of  Tokethorpe  (later  Flockthorpe)  lying  in  the 
Forehoe  hundred  "  was  in  several  parts,  "  two  of  which 
belonged  to  Cossey."  This  same  manor  of  Flockthorpe 
was  possessed  by  the  Cushings  for  several  generations 
thereafter. 

The  Cashing  Arms. 

The  Cushings  of  Norfolk,  Eng.,  were  entitled  to  bear 
arms  for  many  successive  generations  through  their  hold- 
ing the  manors  of  Chosely,  Hardingham,  etc.  During 
this  time  of  course  the  arms  were  repeatedly  *  differenced  * 
by  different  branches.  Therefore  the  attempt  to  ascertain 
the  exact  coat-of-arms  borne  by  the  branch  which  came

GENEALOGY 


EARLY  ANCESTRY 


The  remote  ancestry  of  the  Cashing  family  has  been  the 
subject  of  a  number  of  investigations  which  have  succeeded 
in  tracing  the  family  to  very  early  times.  The  first  work  of 
importance  was  undertaken  by  the  Hon.  Caleb  Cushing. 
He  traced  the  family  to  Norfolk  Co.,  Eng. ,  and  finding  him- 
self unable  to  giv^e  the  necessar}^  time  to  the  research,  engag- 
ed the  late  H.  G.  Somerby  of  London,  a  well  known  genea- 
logist, to  continue  it.  Mr.  Somerby  entered  on  the  task 
with  enthusiasm,  as  evidenced  by  his  letters,  some  of  which 
are  in  the  writer's  possession.  During  the  years  1851-1853 
he  examined  the  ancient  manuscripts  in  the  British  Museum, 
the  Subsidy  Rolls  and  Heraldic  Visitations  for  Norfolk,  the 
parish  registers  and  ancient  deeds  and  wills  connected  with 
various  estates  and  manors  in  Hardingham,  Hingham,  and 
other  places.  His  efforts  were  crowned  with  unexpected 
success  ;  he  established  the  fact  that  the  Cushings  were  one 
of  the  leading  families  in  Norfolk  County  during  the  15th 
and  1 6th  centuries,  being  lords  of  numerous  manors, 
and  he  published  his  results  in  several  important  papers 
before  historical  and  genealogical  societies  in  Great  Britain. 

The  late  Mr.  Lemuel  Cushing,  having  received  the  papers 
and  correspondence  relating  to  the  subject  from  the  Hon. 
Caleb  Cushing,  continued  the  work,adding  many  details, and 
published  the  whole  in  the  first  edition  of  the  Genealogy  of 
the  Cushing  Family  in  1877.  ^^  ^^^^  work  he  traces  the 
family  back  to  Thomas  Cushing  of  Hardingham,  Norfolk 
Co.,  who  lived  in  the  early  part  of  the  15th  century. 


1 4  THE  GENEALOGY  OF  THE 


After  Mr.  lyemuel  Gushing' s  death,  Mr.  Frank  Hamilton 
Gushing  continued  the  investigation,  assi.sted  by  various 
recent  publications  on  the  early  history  of  Norfolk  Gounty, 
and  obtained  valuable  evidence  of  the  descent  of  the  Gushings 
from  the  DeLimisi  family  who  owned  numerous  manors  in 
Norfolk  Gount}^  in  the  nth  and  12th  centuries.  His  early 
decease  interrupted  the  work,  but,  through  the  kindness  of 
his  widow,  the  papers  containing  the  results  of  his  work 
were  submitted  to  the  present  writer.  As  one  or  two  links 
of  the  chain  are  still  missing,  it  was  thought  best  to  publish 
Mr.  Frank  Hamihon  Gushing's  manuscript  verbatim,  in  the 
hope  that  at  some  future  time  the  w^ork  may  be  completed, 
and  to  commence  the  genealogy  of  the  family  at  a  point  from 
which  the  actual  descent  from  father  to  son  rests  on  direct 
documentary  evidence. 

Mr.  Gushing's  manuscript  is  as  follows  : 

"  In  the  Scandinavian  Sagas  relating  to  the  latter  half 
of  the  Eighth  Gentur}^ — 750-800,  A.D. — which  may  be  re- 
garded as  the  period  in  which  reliable  Norse  History  begins, 
frequent  mention  may  be  found  of  the  Viking  Hrolf  Nefja 
Jarl  and  his  ancestors  iuThrondjem  and  the  Maeras  of  Nor- 
way ;  and  in  later  centuries,  of  his  descendants  in  Normandy 
and  England  as  well. 

According  to  these  Sagas,  and  the  earliest  Norman 
accounts,  Hrolf  Nefja,  (i),  had  at  least  one  son  Malahjulc, 
(2);  and  a  daughter,  Hild  or  Ragnhild.  The  daughter  mar- 
ried Rognvald  Maera-Jarl,  who,  in  return  for  assistance 
rendered  by  him  to  Harald  (or  Harold)  Fair  Hair,  in  the 
conquest  of  Norway,  was  made  chief  ruler  over  not  onl}^  the 
two  Maeras,  but  also  Ramsdal.  They  had  three  sons  and 
a  daughter.  The  second  son,  Gongu  Hrolf  (Walking 
Kelt),  became  early  a  great  Viking  leader,  especially  in  the 
East.  Returning  from  one  of  his  expeditions  soon  aiter 
Harald' s   conquest,    he   committed   acts  of  depredation  in 


GUSHING  FAMILY  1  5 


Vikin.  King  Harald,  who  was  then  in  Vikin,  was  very- 
angry  when  he  heard  of  this,  for  he  had  strictly  forbidden 
robber}^  within  his  land.  He  therefore  announced  at  a 
Thing  that  he  made  Hrolf  an  outlaw  fiom  Norway.  When 
Hrolt's  mother  Hild  heard  this  she  went  on  behalf  of  her 
family  to  the  King  to  ask  for  pardon  for  Hrolf;  but  the  King 
was  so  angry  that  her  pra3'ers  were  of  no  avail.  Hence 
Hrolf,  accompanied  by  his  uncle  Malahjulc,  as  Councillor, 
and  a  numerous  following  of  disaffected  Hersirs  sailed  for 
the  Hebrides  ;  whence  they  made  coiiquests,  ultimately  gain- 
ing from  Valland  (now  France),  about  912  A.  D.,  the 
great  Jarls'  realm,  known  soon  after  as  Normandi. 

Thus  Hrolf,  so  well  known  in  later  history  as  Rollo, 
became  the  founder  and  first  Earl  or  Duke  ot  Normandy,  es- 
tablishing,according  to  nearness  of  kin  with  his  own  and  the 
families  of  his  chief  leaders,  the  great  Ruda-jarls  (or  feudal 
nobility  of  Ruen),  ancestors  of  the  Sovereign  families  and 
Norman  Barons  of  Normandy  and  England  alike,  in  later 
centuries. 

In  this  manner  MalahjSilc  became  possessed  of  Toesini 
and  Conches  ;  and  is  referred  to  in  old  records  as  Malahul-

1.  WILLIAM  GUSHING.  (Cussyn  or  Cusseyii),  wasborn

Norfolk  Co.,  Eng.,  who  is  mentioned  in  the  Subsidy  Rolls 
for  Norfolk  in  1327.  He  added  to  the  original  estate  in

8.  MATTHEW  '  GUSHING,  son  of  Peter  and  Susan 
(Hawes)  Gushing,  was  baptized  in  Hardingham,  Kng., 
2  March,  1589.  He  married,  5  August,  1613,  Nazareth, 
daughter  of  Henry  Pitcher,  of  the  famous  family  of  Ad- 
miral Pitcher  of  England.  She  was  baptized  30  Oct.,  1586, 
and  died  in  Hingham,  Mass.,  6  Jan.,  1682.  Matthew 
Gushing  died  30  Sept.,  1660.  For  the  first  fifty  A^ears  of  his 
life  he  lived  in  Hardingham  and  Hingham,  Norfolk  Gounty, 
Eng.,  until  1638,  when  with  his  wife  and  five  children,  and 
his  wife's  sister  (Widow  Francis  Riecroft,  who  died  a  few 
weeks  after  their  arrival )  he  embarked  in  the  ship  "Diligent' ' 
of  Ipswich,  350  tons,  John  Martin,  master,  which  sailed 
from  Gravesend,  26  April,  1638,  with  133  passengers,  among 
whom  was  Robert  Peck,  M.A.,  Rector  of  the  parish  of 
Hingham,  Eng.  The  immediate  occasion  of  their  departure 
seems  to  have  been  trouble  in  ecclesiastical  matters.  Their 
rector,  doubtless  with  the  sympathy  and  aid  of  most  of  those 
constituting  the  emigrating  part}',  had  pulled  down  the  rails 
of  chancel  and  altar,  and  levelled  the  latter  a  foot  below  the 
church,  as  it  remains  to  this  da^^  Being  prosecuted  by 
Bishop  Wren,  he  left  the  Kingdom,  together  with  his  friends 
— who  sold  their  estates  at  half  their  real  value.  The  party, 
having  landed  at  Boston.  Mass.,  10  Aug.,  1638,  immediatel}^ 
proceeded  to  their  destination,  Hingham,  Mass.,  so  named 
after  the  name  of  the  former  home  of  the  Gushing  family  in 
England.     x\t  a  town  meeting  held  1638,  a  house  lot  of  five

acres,  first  below  Pear  Tree  Hill,  on  Bachelor  (Main)  St., 
was  given  to  Matthew  Gushing,  and  it  continued  in  the 
posssession  of  the  family  until  1887.  He  was  early  engaged 
in  the  public  affairs  of  the  town,  became  a  deacon  in  Rev. 
Hobart's  church,  and  was  the  progenitor  of  many  eminent 
descendants.  It  is  now  a  pretty  well  established  fact  that, 
with  the  exception  of  a  few  families  who  have  come  to  this 
country  during  the  past  century,  all  the  persons  bearing  the 
surname  of  Gushing  in  the  United  States  and  Ganada  are 
his  direct  lineal  descendants.  His  will,  which  was  a  verbal 
one,  was  written  after  his  decease  by  his  children,  who,  un- 
der date  of  15  Nov.,  1660,  pray  that  Daniel  Gushing,  Esq., 
their  oldest  brother,  may  be  appointed  administrator  of  their 
father's  estate.      (For  his  will  see  the  appendix.)

10.  JOHN -GUSHING  (Matthew 'j  Avas  born  in  Hing- 
ham,  Eng.,  in  1627.  He  married  in  Hingham,  Mass.,  20 
Jan.,  1658,  Sarah,  daughter  of  Matthew  and  Margaret 
Hawke.  Her  father  was  third  town  clerk  of  Hingham, 
Mass.  She  was  baptized  in  Hingham,  i  Aug.,  1641,  and 
died  in  Scituate,  Mass.,  9  March,  1679.  John  Gushing  died 
in  Scituate  31  March,  1708.  Goming  out  from  England  in 
1638,  he  appears  to  have  remained  in  Hingham,  Mass.,  until 
after  his  father's  death  in  1660.  In  1657  ^^^>  together  with 
Matthias  Briggs,  purchased  for  ^120  the  Vansall  Estate  at 
"Belle  House  Neck",  Scituate,  which  consisted  of  120 
acres  with  house  and  barns.  He  did  not  move  there,  how- 
ever, until  about  1662.  The  land  on  which  the  farm  was 
situated  was  always  known  as  ' '  Belle  House  Neck  " ,  a  name 
given  to  the  place  in  consequence  of  a  bell  that  hung  at  the 
house  there,  for  a  century,  to  give  an  alarm  to  the  neigh- 
boring country  in  case  of  the  approach  of  Indians.  In  1663 
he  was  surveyor  of  highways  and  in  1667,  receiver  of  excivSes. 
He  was  deputy  to  the  colony  in  1674,  and  was  often  re- 
elected. In  1673,  he  was  on  the  committee  for  dividing 
Scituate  lands  ;  and  in  1676,  was  chosen  to  report  to  the 
Government  a  statement  of  all  services  of  the  soldiers  of 
Scituate  in  the  war  with  King  Philip.  Selectman  from  1674 
to  1686  inclusive,  and  Gounty  Magistrate  (Plymouth  Go.) 
1685  to  1692.  Assistant  of  the  Old  Golony  Government  of 
Pl3miouth  Golony  1689  to  1691,  and  representative  to  the 
General  Gourt  at  Boston  in  1692  (the  first  3^ear  after  the  two 
colonies,  Plymouth  and  Massachusetts,  were  united),  and 
for  several  succeeding  years,  Member  of  the  Gouncil  1706 
and  T707.   He  was  also  Golonel  of  the  Plymouth  Regiment.

to  Cape  Elizabeth  (then  Fahnouth),  Me.  Was  coroner  in 
1727  and  1729.  The  house  in  which  he  Hved  at  Cushing's 
Point,  now  in  South  Portland,  was  still  standing  in  1760, 
He  owned  Cushing's  Island  in  Portland  Harbor,  and  sold 
it  to  Joshua  Bangs,  14  Sept.,  1760,  by  Avhose  name  it  was

was  extensively  engaged  in  the  fisheries  and  the  West  India 
trade,  owning  many  schooners  and  sloops.  His  large  mer- 
cantile establishment  was  on  the  point  bearing  his  name,  a 
few  rods  east  of  the  breakwater  and  at  the  western  extremity 
of  the  sandy  cove  west  of  Fort  Preble.  It  is  authoritatively 
stated  that  during  his  time,  there  was  more  commercial  busi- 
ness carried  on  on  the  Cape  Elizabeth  shore  than  on  the 
Falmouth  side.  He  was  active  and  prominent  in  the 
affairs  of  the  settlement,  and  became  one  of  the  most  respected 
as  well  as  distinguished  men  in  Portland  neighborhood. 
He  commanded  the  regiment  of  thecount}^  then  the  highest 
office  in  Maine,  and  in  1757  was  able  to  furnish  50  men 
from  his  regiment  to  defend  the  inhabitants  from  the  Indians 
and  afterwards  provide  100  to  protect  the  Commissioners 
when  arranging  terms  of  peace  with  them.  Was  selectman 
of  the  town  nine  years,  and  justice  of  the  peace  1756,  1760 
and  1 76 1  ;  Justice  of  the  Court  of  Common  Pleas  1760  to 
1763,  and  filled  other  important  offices.  Gov.  Shirley  dined 
at  Col.  Cushing's  23  July,  1754.  He  took  a  prominent  part 
in  the  religious  dissensions  which  broke  out  in  the  Church 
there,  and  in  1756  was  a  leader  of  the  opposition  to  the 
installation  of  the  Rev.  Ephraim  Clark  over  the  Chujch. 
After  the  installation  he  was  set  off  to  the  first  parish 
where  he  afterwards  attended,  though  just  previous  to  his

moderator  of  .their  famous  town  meetings,  and  was  moderator 
of  the  town   meeting  3   Sept.,    1742,    when    Boston   voted

thanks  to  Peter  Faneuil,  Esq.,  for  the  gift  of  the  Market

119.  JACOB  '  CUSHING  (Job  '  Matthew  '  Daniel  -  Mat- 
thew 0  was  born  in  Shrewsbury,  Mass.,  17  Feb.,  1730. 
Married,  8  Nov.,  1753,  Anna,  daughter  of  Rev.  Wareham 
Williams  (of  Waltham,  Mass.)  whom  he  succeeded  as  pastor. 
She  was  born  24  May,  1732.  Jacob  Gushing  graduated  from 
Harvard  College  in  1748.  He  was  elected  Minister  of  Wal- 
tham, 27  July,  1752,  and  ordained,  22  Nov.,  1752.  He  was 
remarkable  for  his  talent  of  prudently  managing  affairs,  both 
temporal  and  spiritual.  He  was  accurate  and  methodical  in 
all  he  did.  He  kept  an  accurate  account  of  the  deaths  hap- 
pening in  Waltham  for  56  years,  1752- 1809  "His  whole 
life  furnished  his  parishioners  no  occasion  for  uneasiness  or 
complaint.  He  died  after  a  short  illness  of  a  day  or  two  on 
Wednesday,  18  Jan.,  1809,  in  the  79th  3^ear  of  his  age,  and 
57th  of  his  ministry.  He  had  enjoyed  through  life  an  un- 
common stock  of  health— had  preached  at  Weston  the  Sab- 
bath before  his  death  with  unabated  vigor.  He  was  venerable 
for  years  and  piety,  his  praise  was  in  all  the  churches,  and 
as  a  just  tribute  to  his  w^orth  as  a  divine  and  the  dignity  of 
his  character,  in  1806,  the  degree  of  D.D.  was  conferred  upon 
him  by  the  University  of  Cambridge  ".

yet  social  with  all.  He  was  a  man  of  large  stature  and  frame. 
In  his  last  years  with  his  flowing  white  locks  and  faded  worn 
features  his  appearance  was  truly  venerable.  He  was  much 
beloved  by  the  good  people  of  the  town,  and  his  Hfe  was  so 
irreproachable  that  he  had  the  true  respect  of  all.  His  in- 
fluence being  that  of  a  gentle,  exemplary,  and  faithful  teacher 
and  friend  was  unchallenged,  and  extending  through  so  many 
years  had  an  almost  unconscious  moulding  power,  which 
has  been  very  great  upon  the  town." 

(Address  of  Rev.  J.  J.  Crosby.)

leaving  no  descendants.  Graduated  from  Harvard  College

tice in  Pownalboro',  which  then  comprehended  the  towns 
of  Dresden  and  Wiscassett,  residing  with  his  brother  Charles, 
and  continued  his  practice  there  until  elevated  to  the  Bench. 
Of  all  the  Judges  and  Officers  of  the  Courts  in  the  three 
counties  and  of  the  County  Officers  he  was  the  solitary  law- 
yer, he  stood  alone  as  an  educated  lawyer  in  this  spacious 
territory  and  the  first  who  settled  in  Maine  He  was  one  of 
the  six  lawyers  in  Maine  who  were  raised  to  the  degree  of 
Barrister.  He  was  for  a  time  Attorney  General  of  Mass.  ; 
in  1768,  was  appointed  the  first  Judge  of  Probate  in  Lincoln 
County  and  in  1772  made  Judge  of  the  Superior  Court.  At 
the  re-organization  of  the  Superior  Court,  Mass.,  1777,  he  was 
appointed  Chief  Justice  of  the  Court,  the  first  who  held  the 
office  under  the  free  Government  of  the  Commonwealth  and 
labored  with  great  success  in  establishing  the  judicial  system 
on  a  firm  basis.  He  became  Judge  of  the  Supreme  Judicial 
Court,  1782.  At  the  beginning  of  the  Revolution,  he  alone 
among  the  high  in  office  supported  the  rights  of  the  Revolu- 
tionists He  was  Vice-President  of  the  Mass.  Convention 
which  ratified  the  U.  S.  Constitution  in  1788.  He  was 
the  first  Chief  Justice  of  the  State  under  this  Constitution, 
and  at  the  organization  of  the  U.  S.  Government  in  1789  he 
was  selected  by  Washington  as  an  Associate  Justice  of  theU.S. 
Supreme  Court,  in  which  office  he  eminently  shone.  While  As- 
sociate Judge,  he  was  accompanied  in  his  circuit  by  Mrs.  Cush- 
ing  ;  he  drove  a  phaeton  and  a  pair  of  horses  and  was  followed 
b}^  his  negro  man  "Prince' '  on  horseback.  During  the  mission 
of  Chief  Justice  John  Jay,  Envoy  Extraordinary  to  the  Court 
of  Great  Britain,  negotiating  the  famous  treaty  with  that 
Country,  Judge  Cushing  presided,  and  as  Senior  Justice  ad-

ministered  the  oath  of  office  to  Washington  at  the  beginning 
of  his  second  term  as  President,  4  March,  1793.    In  1794  he 
was  a  candidate  for  Governor  of  Mass. ,   a  rival  of  Samuel 
Adams.     John  Adams  said  of  him  :    "I  shall  be  happier  if 
Gushing  succeeds,  and  the  State  will  be  more  prudently  con- 
ducted."    In   1796,  after  Judge  Jay's  resignation,  he  was 
nominated  by  Washington  to  the  Chief  Justice  office,  and  this 
offer  was  unanimously  confirmed  by  the  Senate,    27  Jan., 
1796,  and  on  the  evening  of  the  same  day  was  invited  to  a 
large  dinner  party  at  the  President's.     As  he  entered  the 
room,  Washington  from  the  head  of  the  table  turned  to  him 
and  said  with  great  impressiveness  ;   "The  Chief  Justice  of 
the  United  States  will  please  take  his  seat  on  my  right."    It 
is  said  that  this  was  the  first  intimation  that  Cushing  had  of 
his  selection.    Nothing  but  a  confidence  in  his  ability  and  in 
his  unshaken  integrity  could  have  united  contending  parties 
on  that  occasion  ;  but  notwithstanding  this  extraordinarj^ 
expression  of  confidence,  he  declined  the  office  on  account  of 
infirm  health,  but  continued  on  the  bench  until   18 10,  when 
he  had  prepared  an  instrument  of  resignation,  but  was  called 
to  resign  life.     He  was  a  man  of  tall  and  dignified  presence, 
and  as  he  moved  along  the  streets  with  his  cocked  hat,  bush 
wig  and  small   clothes,   he  made  an  imposing  appearance 
which  attracted  general  attention.     He  was  the  last  Chief 
Justice  who  wore  the  large  wig  of  the  English  Judges.     As 
a  Judge  he  was  eminently  quahfied  by  his  learning  and  not 
less  by  his  unshaken  integrity  and  deliberate  temper.     It  is 
said  of  him  in  i8or,  that  he  performed  the  duties  of  his  high 
office  with  order  and  perspicuity  and  guided  the  bar  with 
mild,  though  commanding  dignity.     In  private  life  he  was 
all  that  was  amiable,  always  ready  to  instruct  by  useful  dis- 
course and  to  make  his  friends  happy  with  his  cheerfulness. 
He  diligently  collected  works  of  taste  and  (if  we  may  judge 
by  the  numerous  notes  written  with  his  own  hand  in  mar-

gius)  he  read  wiLli  the  greatest  care.  He  was  a  founder  and 
member  of  the  Americm  Academy  of  Arts  and  Sciences.  He 
was  a  learned  theologian,  wellacquainted  wnth  the  controver- 
sies of  the  da}',  and  though  far  from  gathering  heat  in  those 
controversies,  was  conspicuousl}^  on  the  side  of  liberal  Chris- 
tianit}'.  As  an  exemplary  Christian,  he  was  irreproachable, 
and  as  a  public  character,  he  is  universally  acknowledged  to 
have  stood  in  the  first  rank  of  his  countrymen. 

A  massive  granite  boulder  marks  the  spot  of  his  burial  on 
"  Belle  House  Neck  "  in  Scituate.

with  two  portraits  of  General  Washington  and  John  Adams,

in  America,  made  a  number  of  portraits  of  distinguished 
people.     These  are  still  valued  for  their  character  and  truth.

the  battles  of  Gharlestow^n ,  S.  G.,  Yorktown,  Va.,  etc.,  and

March,  1809,  he  was  collector  of  the  Port  of  Boston.  He 
was  also  President  of  the  Societ}^  of  the  Gincinnati.  At  his 
funeral  his  pall  was  borne  by  the  Hon.  John  Adams,  Hon.

Honor  Lieut.  Governor  Gobb  and  Thomas  Melleville,  Esq. 
The  bells  in  Boston  and  other  places  were  tolled  for  an  hour. 
He  resided  in  Hingham.

143.  THOMAS  '  GUSHING  (Thomas  *  John  ^"^  Mat- 
thew ^  )  was  born  m  Boston,  Mass.,  24  March,  1725.  He 
married,  i  Oct.,  1747,  Deborah  Fletcher,  who  died  1790,  ae. 
63.  He  died  28  Feb.,  1788.  Graduated  from  Harvard 
College  in  1744  ;  A.  M.  ;  L.  L.  D.  1785  ;  also  Yale  1750. 
Fellow  of  the  American  Acadeni}-. 

Representative  to  the  General  Court  in  1761,  re-elected  in 
1762  and  up  to  1769  inclusive  ;  was  elected  Speaker  of  the 
General  Court,  26  Ma}^  1768,  and  was  Speaker  of  the 
House  of  Representatives  from  1766  to  1774  inclusive,  and 
rose  to  higher  honors  in  the  State  than  either  his  father  or 
grandfather.  On  18  Dec,  1765,  he  was  appointed  with 
others  a  committee  to  sign  and  present  a  Memorial  to  the 
Governor  in  Council,  protesting  against  the  shutting  up  of 
the  Courts  of  Law  and  other  infringements  upon  the  liber- 
ties of  the  people.  He  was  friend  ^nd  co-worker  in  the 
patriot  cause  with  Adams,  Otis,  and  Warren.  When  Otis 
who  had  been  chosen  Speaker  was  negatived  b}^  the  govern- 
ment (in  1764)  he  was  elected  in  his  place,  filling  it  until 
1774,  when  he  was  a  member  of  the  Provincial  Congress, 
and  of  the  Congress  which  met  at  Philadelphia.  On  his 
return  he  was  elected  to  the  Council ;  w^as  Commissary- 
general  from  1775  to  1779,  (see  interesting  letter  from  him 
to  John  Hancock,  dated  3  May,  1776,  to  be  found  in  Histo- 
rical Magazine,  Boston,  i860,  p.  345)  ;  Judge  of  the  Court 
of  Common  Pleas,  and  of  Probate,  in  Suffolk  Co.,  in  1777  ; 
declined  a  seat  in  the  Continental  Congress,  in  1779,  and 
was  Lieut. -Governor  of  Mass.  under  Hancock  and  Bowdoin, 
from  1779  until  his  death,  and  Acting- Governor  in  1785. 
His  signature  being  affixed  to  all  public  papers,  as  Speaker 
of  the  House,  caused  him  to  be  regarded  in  Great  Britain  as 
the  leader  of  the  Whigs  in  this  country.  In  Dr.  Johnson's 
pamphlet  "  Taxation  no  Tyranny  ",  one  object  of  the  Ame- 


104  THE  GENEALOGY  OF  THE 

ricans  is  said  to  be  "  to  adorn  the  brows  of  Mr.  Gushing 
with  a  diadem."  He  was  the  devoted  friend  and  counsellor 
of  Hancock,  and  the  friend  and  correspondent  of  Franklin, 
from  whom  he  received  the  letters  of  Hutchison  and  others, 
that  produced  so  great  effect  at  that  time.  He  was  Com- 
missioner of  the  Societ}^  in  London  for  Propagating  the  Gos- 
pel in  New  England,  and  one  of  the  founders  of  the  American 
Acadeni}^  of  Arts  and  Sciences.  "He  was  moderate  and  con- 
ciliatory in  character,  his  good  sense  and  sound  judgment, 
the  urbanit}^  of  his  manners,  his  universal  good  character, 
his  numerous  friends  and  connections,  and  his  continual  in- 
tercourse with  all  sorts  of  people,  added  to  his  constant 
attachment  to  the  liberties  of  his  countr}^  gave  him  great  and 
salutary  influence  from  the  beginning,  in  1760."  Drake's 
Diet.  Amer.  Biog. 

He  was  from  youth  a  professor  of  religion,  the  motives 
of  the  gospel  governed  him  through  life,  and  at  the  hour  of 
his  departure  from  the  world  its  sublime  doctrines  and  its 
promises  gave  him  support  '•'  "^  ^\  He  was  charitable  to  the 
poor  and  amiable  in  all  the  relations  of  life.  His  days  were 
passed  in  constant  exertion  for  the  public  good."  Funeral 
Sermon. 

He  was  buried  in  the  Granary  Burying  Ground,  Boston, 
where  a  mural  tablet  was  erected  with  the  Gushing  Goat  of 
Arms  on  it.      (See  p.  10.)

145.  CHARLES  '  GUSHING  (Jacob  *  Matthew  '  John  ' 
Matthew^)  was  born  in  Hingham,  Mass.,  13  July,  1744. 
He  married  at  Halifax,  Mass.,  23  Feb.,  1769,  Hannah, 
daughter  of  Thomas  and  Rachel  (Gushing)  Croade 
(No.  57  :  ii).  He  died  25  Nov.,  1809.  Was  a  farmer  and 
magistrate. 

He  was  a  member  of  the  Committee  of  Correspondence 
1779-81,  and  served  with  the  Continental  Army  all  through 
the  Revolutionary  War.  As  Captain  of  a  Hingham  com- 
pany in  Gen.  Thomas'  command,  he  was  in  the  expedition 
to  Canada,  and  saved  his  company  from  the  ravages  of 
small-pox,  so  generally  disastrous  to  the  army  in  that  expe- 
dition by  the  then  7c/ffa  proceeding  of  innoculation.  He 
returned  on  horseback  across  the  Hoosac  Ridge.  After- 
wards, Colonel  of  a  Continental  Regiment.  Representative 
1 780-8 1 -84-90-9 1 -92-93,  and  member  of  the  Senate  in  1794. 

He  removed  with  his  family,  in  1791,  from  Hingham  to 
Lunenburg,  Mass.,  and  settled  on  what  has  since  been 
called  the  ' '  Brook  Farm  ' ' ,  about  one  mile  west  of  the  centre 
of  the  town,  where  he  died  in  1809.  His  wife  lived  to  be 
quite  old  wath  her  daughter  Mrs.  Harrington  ;  she  used  to 
say  she  was  the  3'oungest  of  16  sisters.

167.  NATHAN  '  GUSHING  (Joseph  ^"^  John  ^  Matthew  0 
was  born  in  Scituate,  Mass.,  24  Sept..  1742.     He  married, 
II  July,  1772,  Abigail,  daughter  of  Capt.   Christopher  Til- 
den,  of  Pembroke.     She  died  8  Nov.,  18 10,  ^.  65.     He  died 
in  Scituate,  4  Nov.,  1812.  Graduated  from  Harvard  College 
in  1763.     ' '  He  was  first  a  preacher  and  afterwards  a  lawyer. 
He  was  a  delegate  to  the  Plymouth  County  Congress,  held 
at  Plympton,  26  Sept.,  1774,  and  one  of  the  signers  of  the 
Manifesto  issued  at  the  Plymouth   Congress,   4  Oct.,    1774. 
In  1776  he  was  appointed  Judge  of  Admiralty,   and  with 
great  firmness  condemned  the  captured  British  vessels,  which 
brought  him  into  notoriety  as  a  patriot.      He  was  appointed 
Judge  of  the  Supreme  Court  in  1789,  in  which  office  he  con- 
tinued until  1801,  when  he  resigned.     He  was  afterwards  a 
counsellor  of  the  State.     He  was  a  gentleman  of  noble  form, 
commanding  countenance  and  courteous   manners,   distin- 
guished more  for  solid  judgment  and  discretion  than  for 
eloquence."     When  Massachusetts  became  a  State,  action 
was  taken  by  the  Legislatureon  the  subject  of  a  state  seal  and 
under  date  of  13  Dec,  1870,  we  have  the  following  lecord  : 
"  Ordered  that  Nathan  Cushing  be  a  committee  to  prepare 
a  seal  for  the  Commonwealth  of  Massachusetts."   His  report 
was  afterwards  accepted  and  the  device  he  recommended  is 
still  in  use  as  the  Arms  of  Massachusetts-

had  owned  a  large  real  estate  but  disposed  of  it  during  the

equip  a  regiment),  receiving  his  pay  in  Continental  mone}', 
the  depreciation  of  which  reduced  him  to  poverty.  In  1799

Pa.,  of  the  ship  "  Good  Intent",  the  first  ever  built  on  Lake 
Erie.  From  1792-1805,  he  Hved  in  Paris,  Oneida  Co.,  N,Y., 
whence  he  removed  to  Fredonia,  Chatauqua  Co.,  N.Y., 
where  he  accumulated  a  large  landed  property.  He  there 
commenced  a  nursery  and  set  out  the  oldest  orchard  in  the 
county  and  also  planted  pits  for  peach  trees  and  the  third 
year  after  had  plenty  of  that  fruit.  He  was  a  Baptist  and 
instrumental  in  organizing  and  establishing,  in  1808,  one 
of  the  first  churches  of  that  denomination  in  the  County. 
He  was  appointed  in  1808  an  Associate  Judge  of  the  newly 
formed  count}'  of  Chatauqua,  which  for  three  years  was 
united  with  the  adjoining  counties  of  Niagara  and  Erie,  the 
Court  meeting  at  Bufialo.  The  first  Court  of  Common  Pleas 
and  General  Sessions  of  the  Peace  in  the  new  County  of 
Niagara  was  held  by  Judge  Zattu  Cushing  in  June,  1808,  in 
Landlord's  Tavern,  Buffalo  (or  New  AmvSterdam),  and  was 
held  there  until  the  Court  House  and  Jail  were  erected.  He 
was  the  leading  member  of  the  Court  and  in  181 1,  when  the 
organization  of  Chatauqua  Co.  was  completed,  he  w^as  ap- 
pointed first  Judge  of  it.  In  1822,  he  retired  from  the  Bench 
with  the  reputation  of  an  upright,  dignified,  clear-headed 
Judge.  His  intuitive  perception  of  justice  and  his  strong 
common-sense  had  well  supplied  the  place  of  extended  legal 
learning. 

In  person  he  w^as  tall  and  commanding.  He  was  from  his 
3'outh  a  zealous  active  Christian,  an  earnest,  energetic 
speaker,  and  eminently  benevolent  to  the  poor  and  need5^ 
His  portrait  is  suspended  in  the  Chatauqua  Co.  Court  House 
in  Mayville,  the  County  seat.

230.  GEORGE  RUSSELL"  GUSHING  (David ^  AbeP 
Theophil lis  ^  Daniel  -  Matthew  0  was  born  in  Hingham, 
Mass.,  24  April,  1768.  He  married,  first,  13  Aug.,  1801, 
Catharine,  daughter  of  Jacob  Willard.  She  died  28  April,

in  1800.  In  early  life  he  was  a  seafaring  man  and  com-

to  remain  in  France  on  account  of  the  embargo  laid  upon 
his  vessel.  He  visited  all  the  noted  seaports  of  the  world, 
and  amassed  something  of  a  fortune.  He  had  a  miniature 
of  himself  painted  in  London,  Eng.,  with  the  Gushing  Goat 
of  Arms  upon  its  back,  which  is  now  in  the  possession  of 
his  immediate  descendants.  He  was  a  justice  of  the  peace 
of  Ashburnham  for  a  number  of  years  ;  also  elected  Gaptain 
of  a  Gompany  in  the  4th  Regiment  of  Infantry,  2nd  Brigade, 
7th  Division  of  the  militia.

252.  THOMAS  CROADE  "  GUSHING  (Benjamin  '  So- 
lomon ^  Matthew  ^  Daniel  -  Matthew  ^)  was  born  in  Hing-

Gushing  died  in  Salem,  Mass.,  Sept.,  1824.  He  was 
a  printer  by  profession,  having  served  his  apprenticeship 
with  Samuel  Hull,  Editor  of  the  "  Salem  Gazette  ".  Upon 
the  expiration  of  his  apprenticeship,  he  began  a  paper  at 
Gharlestown,  under  the  title  of  the  "  American  Recorder  and 
Gharlestown  Advertiser  ",  but  he  soon  removed  to  Salem, 
Essex  Go.,  Mass.,  where  he  established  his  paper  under  the 
title  of  the  ' '  Salem  Mercury  ' ' ,  the  first  number  of  which 
was  issued  14  Oct.,  1786.  On  i  Jan.,  1790,  the  name  of  the 
paper  was  changed  to  the  ' '  Salem  Gazette  ' '  and  Mr.  Gush- 
ing continued  to  edit  it  until  1822,  when  his  infirm  health 
obliged  him  to  relinquish  his  agency  in  it.  He  conducted 
his  paper  with  ability  and  with  a  steadfast  and  conscientious 
adherence  to  Whig  principles.  He  also  kept  a  book- store 
in  partnership  with  Mr.  John  Appleton  under  the  name  of 
' '  Gushing  &  Appleton  " .

He  was  a  lawyer  and  a  man  of  brilliant  mind.  One  of 
the  resolutions  at  the  meeting  of  the  bar  after  his  death 
expresses  in  few  words  the  estimation  in  which  he  was  held 
by  his  fellow  tow^nsmen  :  "  Resolved,  that  we,  as  his  friends 
and  brethren  in  the  legal  profession,  bear  our  united  testimony 
to  his  high  sense  of  honor,  to  the  kindness  and  courtesy 
which  ever  marked  all  his  intercourse  with  us,  to  the  clear- 
ness and  vigor  of  his  mind,  which  had  been  cultivated  with 
assiduous  care  and  enriched  by  treasures  drawn  from  ever}^ 
field  of  literature,  to  the  elevation  and  purity  of  his  taste, 
to  the  cultivated  humor  and  generous  social  impulses  which 
made  him  the  life  and  pride  of  every  circle,  and  to  that  innate 
modesty  which  veiled  ability  and  worth  from  the  stranger,

is  now  Kempt,  but  was  then  an  unbroken  wilderness  for  80 
miles.  He  hewed  out  a  clearing  to  build  a  house,  and 
brought  his  young  wife  40  miles  on  horseback.  His  daughter 
saj^s  :  "  I  have  heard  him  tell  so  many  times  of  their  pioneer 
life  ;  when  sometimes  he  had  to  leave  his  wife  alone  for 
more  than  a  week  with  her  young  baby,  my  oldest  brother. 
Other  families  settled  eight  miles  nearer  the  seaboard,  and

of  So.  Scituate,  Mass.  She  died  at  Winterport,  Me.,  4  Aug.,

engaged  largely  in  the  lumbering  business  ;  was  the  pioneer 
in  Eastern  Maine  of  the  manufacture  and  exportation  of 
sugar  box  shooks  to  the  West  Indies.  Many  of  the  shooks 
were  sent  from  his  mill  at  St.  John,  N.  B. ,  which  in  partnership 
with  his  brother  Andre,  as  Andre  Cushing  &  Co.,  he  built 
in  1 85 1  on  Union  Point,  opposite  the  St.  John  River  falls. 
He  served  several  sessions  a.^  a  member  of  the  Legislature 
of  Maine,  as  Representative  of  his  town  in  the  House  of  Re- 
presentatives, and  as  Senator  from  the  County  of  Waldo. 
He  was  a  prominent  and  earnest  advocate  of  tempf  ranee 
and  anti-slaver}'  causes  in  their  early  and  unpopular  days. 
In  1 87 1  he  caused  to  be  erected  a  beautiful  granite  monu- 
ment dedicated  to  the  Soldiers  and  Sailors  of  the  War  of  the 
Rebellion  who  had  enlisted  from  the  town  of  Winterport, 
and  presented  it  as  a  free  gift  to  the  town.

525.  LEMUEIv '  eUSHING  (Job  ^-*  Matthew  '  Daniel  ^ 
Matthew  ^ )  was  born  at  Three  Rivers,  Que.,  26  April,  1806. 
He  married,  25  Aug.,  1836,  Catherine,  daughter  of  John  S. 
Hutchins  of  Lachute.  Que.  She  w^as  born  13  April,  1816, 
and  died  11  Feb.,  1903.  having  lived  to  the  advanced  age 
of  88  years.  During  the  greater  part  of  her  life  she  took  a 
keen  interest  in  the  politics  of  her  country,  was  very  hospi- 
table and  generous  hearted,  a  good  friend  to  all  and  an  earnest 
helper  in  the  temperance  cause.  Lemuel  Gushing  died  18  May, 
1875.  He  was  one  of  the  pioneers  in  the  settlement  of  the 
Ottawa  Valley,  having  removed  in  early  youth  to  the  lum- 
bering district  of  Chatham,  on  the  Ottawa  River,  50  miles 
above  Montreal.  Although  then  (1823)  but  sixteen  years 
old  he  opened  a  store  and  commenced  business  for  himself 
with  a  very  small  capital.  He  underwent  man}^  severe 
trials,  but  possessed  of  indomitable  energy  and  perseverance 
and  a  vigorous  constitution  he  successfully  overcame  them 
all  and  attained  to  considerable  wealth  and  prominence.  He 
acted  as  Justice  of  the  Peace  and  magistrate  for  over  forty 
years,  and  for  many  years  filled  successively  the  offices  of 
Councillor  and  Mayor  of  the  Township  and  Warden  of  the 
Couaty.  On  the  breaking  out  of  the  Canadian  RebeUion  in 
1837,  ^^  armed  a  company  of  volunteers  in  defence  of  the 
British  Flag  and  marched  with  them  to  St.  Eustache  and 
was  instrumental  in  preventing  much  pillage  and  the  des- 
truction of  the  Registry  office  of  St.  Benoit,  in  which  were 
deposited  many  valuable  papers.  He  was  three  times 
owner  of  the  celebrated  Caledonia  Springs,  and  in  1859  P^^^" 
chased  the  property  known  as  Cushing's  Island,  Portland, 
Me.

first,  22  Jan.,  18 15,  Aritta  Martin.  She  died  15  Nov.,  1830. 
He  married,  secondly,  25  Oct.,  1831,  Melinda  Peck  Barrows, 
a  descendant  of  William  and  George  Barrows  who  were 
among  the  Mayflower  emigrants.  She  died  16  March,  1870. 
For  his  third  wife  he  married,  26  Nov.,  1870,  Rebecca  Ben- 
son. He. died  in  Providence,  111.,  12  Jan.,  1877.  In  early 
life  he  was  engaged  in  business  as  a  retail*  grocer  in  Provi- 
dence, R.  I.  In  1836,  he  and  two  others  went  west,  and 
travelled  over  the  country  within  a  radius  of  200  miles  from 
Chicago,  in  order  to  find  a  desirable  location,  and  decided  to 
buy  land  where  the  town  of  Providence  now  stands.  The 
next  year.  May,  1837,  about  30  families,  with  their  house- 
hold goods  and  provisions  to  last  one  year,  moved  west  from 
Providence,  R.  I.,  to  Bureau  Co.,  Illinois,  where  a  town  was 
founded  of  the  same  name.  Indians  were  still  to  be  found 
in  lUinois,  but  were  migrating  rapidly  west  of  the  Missis- 
sippi River,  the  Black  Hawk  war  having  just  been  closed. 
He  endured,  with  the  early  pioneers  of  the  West,  many  hard- 
ships and  privations.  He  kept  the  company  store  for  several 
years  and  supplied  the  people  for  miles  around,  going  to 
Chicago,  a  distance  of  140  miles,  for  supplies.  At  one  time, 
he  came  very  near  perishing  in  a  violent  snowstorm,  while 
crossing  the  prairies.

and  North  East,  Pennsylvania,  where  his  children  were  born 
and  where  he  continued  to  reside  until  1861,  w-hen  he  moved 
to  Barre  Centre,  Orleans  Co.,  N.  Y.  During  the  following 
year  Dr.  Cushing  was  appointed  assistant-surgeon  of  the 
Army,  and  served  throughout  the  war,  being  promoted  to 
the  rank  of  Major  and  full  surgeon  in  the  regular  army. 
Soon  after  the  close  of  the  war,  he  resigned  and,  purchasing 
a  farm,  became  a  farmer  and  practising  physician  again. 
With  the  growth  of  his  practice  he  was  compelled  to  reside 
for  a  number  (;f  years  in  Medina,  one  of  the  principal  towns 
of  the  county,  but  ultimateh^  abandoned  practice  and  returned 
to  his  farm  to  seek  retirement  and  leisure  for  historical  and 
philosophical  research  and  writing.

where  the  grandfather  (Judge  Zattii  Gushing)  and  other

There  was  not  a  year  during  the  American  Givil  War  that 
Lieut.  Gushing  did  not  distinguish  himself  by  some  perilous 
adventure.  He  commanded  a  ship  at  nineteen  years  of  age 
and  captured  the  first  prize  of  the  war,  the  "Delaware 
Farmer".  On  the  23  Nov.,  1862,  he  was  ordered  in  the 
^steamer  ' '  Kllis  ' '  to  capture  Jacksonville  and  destroy  the 
Bait  works  in  New  River  Inlet.  After  performing  this 
duty  successfully  the  "Kllis"  got  aground,  Lieut. 
Gushing  fired  her  and  escaped  in  a  small  boat,  receiving 
special  commendation  for  his  cooluess,  courage,  and  conduct 
in  this  affair.  His  most  famous  exploit  was  the  destruction 
of  the  rebel  ram  "Albemarle",  27  Oct.  1864. 

The  following  account  of  this  affair  is  taken  from  Harper's 
Weekly  Magazine,  19  Nov.,  1864. 

' '  The  rebel  ram  ' '  Albemarle  ' '  was  one  of  the  most 
formidable  vessels  which  the  Gonfederate  navy  ever  floated. 
It  played  a  conspicuous  part  in  the  capture  of  Plymouth  last 
spring  and  on  that  occasion  sank  the  Southfield.  She  attacked 
the  Miami  also,  and  a  vShot  from  the  latter,  striking  the  iron 
walls  of  the  ram,  rebounded  and  killed  Gapt.  Flusser  of  the 
Miami,  who  was  an  intimate  friend  of  Lieut.  Gushing.  It  is 
said  that  for  this  reason  Lieut.  Gushing  vowed  vengeance 
against  the  Albemarle. 

"  As  early  as  last  June,  Lieut.  Gushing,  then  commanding 
the  Monticello,  submitted  to  the  Admiral  (Lee)  a  plan  for  the 


GUSHING  FAMILY  38  5 


destruction  of  the  Albemarle.     The  plan  was  approved  and 
the-I^ieutenant  withdrawn  to  perform  this  special  service. 

"  After  the  conception  of  his  plan,  Lieut.  Gushing  came 
to  New  York  and  applied  to  one  of  the  new  steam-packets  a 
torpedo  arrangement  and  returned  to  the  sound. 

"  The  Albemarle  had  been  lying  at  Plymouth  for  some 
weeks  previous  to  its  destruction.  A  mile  below  the  tow^n, 
on  the  wreck  of  the  Southfield,  a  rebel  picket  was  stationed. 
On  the  night  of  Oct.  27,  Gushing,  with  a  company  ot  thir- 
teen men,  proceeded  up  the  Roanoke  River  toward  Plymouth. 
The  distance  from  the  mouth  of  the  river  to  the  ram  was  8 
miles.  The  picket  above  mentioned  was  passed  without 
alarm,  and  the  Albemarle  was  discovered  lying  fast  to  the 
wharf  '  with  logs  around  her  about  30  feet  from  her  side  ' . 
As  the  party  approached  the  rebels  opened  fire  from  the 
shore,  which  was  returned  by  the  steam  launch.  The  ap- 
proach was  made  in  the  form  of  a  circle  and  with  bows  on, 
and  when  the  logs  were  struck  they  were  driven  in  some 
feet,  the  bows  of  the  launch  resting  on  them.  '  The  torpedo- 
boom  was  then  lowered,'  says  Lieut.  Gushing,  'and  by  a 
vigorous  pull,  I  succeeded  in  driving  the  torpedo  under  the 
overhang  and  exploding  it  at  the  same  time  that  the  Albe- 
marle's gun  was  fired.  A  shot  seemed  to  go  crashing  through 
my  boat,  and  a  dense  mass  of  water  rushed  in  from  the  tor- 
pedo, filling  the  launch  and  completely  disabling  her.  The 
enemy  then  continued  his  fire  at  fifteen  feet  range,  and  de- 
manded our  surrender,  which  I  twice  refused,  ordering  the 
men  to  save  themselves,  and  removing  my  overcoat  and 
shoes.  Springing  into  the  river.  I  swam,  with  others,  into 
the  middle  of  the  stream,  the  rebels  failing  to  hit  us.' 
Gushing' s  escape  was  so  precipitate  that  he  was  not  able  to 
report  the  destruction  of  the  ram  from  his  own  observation, 
but  formed  his  judgment  from  a  conversation  which  he  heard 
while  concealed  in  the  marshes  close  to  the  enemy's  fort,  and 


3  8  6  THE  GENEALOGY  OF  THE 

from  the  report  of  a  negro  whom  he  sent  into  town  for  in- 
formation. He  had  become  exhausted  in  swimming,  and 
had  taken  shelter  in  the  immediate  vicinity  of  the  enemy. 
He  was  picked  up  by  the  "  Valley  City"  on  the  night  of 
the  30th,  having  made  his  way  to  that  vessel  in  a  skiff  cap- 
tured from  an  enemy's  picket." 

Five  times  he  was  publicly  thanked  by  the  Navy  Depart- 
ment, and  for  the  Albemarle  affair  received  the  "  Thanks  of 
Congress",  the  highest  honor  the  Government  could  pay. 
He  commanded  the  steamer  "  Maumee",  Asiatic  Squadron, 
1868-9,  He  was  the  3'oungest  man  of  his  rank  in  the  navy, 
but  the;  hardships  of  the  service,  especially  the  two  years' 
work  in  the  blockading  service, — before  he  was  a  man  grown 
— was  too  great  a  .strain  on  his  delicate  nervous  organiza- 
tion, and  was  the  cause  of  his  death  at  the  age  of  thirty-two 
years.

to  Medina,  N.  Y.,  in  1870,  in  a  field  of  rich  material.  He 
extended  his  investigations  to  the  ancient  fortifications, 
burial  grounds  and  camp  sites  of  Madison  and  Onondaga 
Counties.  He  entered  Cornell  University  in  1875,  but  de- 
voted his  time  to  assisting  Dr.  Charles  Rau  in  preparing  the 
Indian  collections  of  the  National  Museum  for  the  Centen- 
nial Exposition  and  was  Curator  of  the  entire  collection 
throughout  the  Exhibition,  after  which  he  became  Curator 
of  the  Ethnological  Department  of  the  National  Museum  in 
Washington,  D.  C.  In  1879,  he  joined  Maj.  J.  W.  Powell, 
U.S.A.,  in  his  expedition  to  New  Mexico,  as  Assistant  of 
the  United  States  Bureau  of  Ethnology  of  the  Smithsonian 
Institute.  Mr.  Cushing,  at  his  own  request,  remained  with 
the  Zuni  Indians,  adopting  their  dress,  customs  and  habits, 
and  in  this  way  for  three  years  studied  their  history  and 
language.  In  his  second  3^ear's  sojourn,  he  was  formally 
adopted  bj^  the  tribe  and  initiated  with  the  sacred  *  *  Priest- 
hood of  the  Bow."  In  1882,  he  escorted  a  party  of  six  Zu- 
nis  to  the  Atlantic  Ocean  or  "  Ocean  of  Sunrise  ",  to  carry 
its  waters  to  their  temple  in  the  Pueblos.  Two  of  the  natives 
remained  with  him  in  Washington  during  the  summer  and 
aided  him  in  preparing  his  contribution  to  the  Bureau  of 
Ethnolog}'  on  Zuni  Fetiches.  He  returned  to  his  Indian 
friends  in  1882.  Failing  health  obhged  him  to  return  to  the 
East,  and  in  1884,  accompanied  by  three  Indians  to  aid  him 
in  the  preparation  of  a  Dictionar}^  and  Grammar  of  the  Zuni 
language,  and  in  translating  m3^th  stories,  songs  and 
rituals,  he  settled  in  Washington.  From  1886  to  1888, 
Mr.  Cushing  organized  and  conducted  archeologic  research 
in  the  Salado  and  Gila  Valleys  in  Arizona,  in  charge  of  the 


Frank  Hamii^ton  Gushing 

of  Zuni  fame.

Hemenwa}^  Southwestern  Archeological  Expedition.  In 
1895,  he  went  to  make  investigations  in  Florida.  The  dis- 
coveries made  by  him  on  this  expedition  were  of  great  in- 
terest and  of  profound  importance  in  American  archeology, 
and  at  his  death  he  had  nearl}^  finished  a  voluminous  report 
on  his  discoveries.  (Lamb's  Biographical  Dictionary,  U.S.,

ranges  even  to  the  borders  of  China,  and  visited  people  who 
are  just  now  coming  into  the  range  of  regular  missionary 
work.     Dr.  Gushing  duplicated  in  the  Shan  language  the 
work  of  Dr.  Adoniram  Judson  in  the  Burman.   He  prepared 
the  first  dictionary  of  the  Shan-English  language  and  trans- 
lated the  whole  Bible  into  Shan.     He  also  made  a  grammar

of  the  Shan  language,  and  wrote  hj-mns,  tracts  and  elemen- 
tary school  books.  On  II  P'eb.,  1895,  he  was  appomted 
President  of  Rangoon  Baptist  College  after  having  served  as 
president  pro  tern,  for  about  two  j^ears.  In  1893  the  school

his  courtesy  and  tact  maintained  amicable  relations  with  the 
representatives  of  the  government  of  India  and  with  the 
diverse  elements  in  the  school.  He  obtained  many  advan- 
tages for  the  College  from  the  government  and  saw  it  steadily 
grow  under  his  fostering  care  to  one  of  the  foremost  educa- 
tional institutions  of  India.  Dr.  Gushing  was  prominent 
not  only  in  the  religious  and  educational,  but  also  in  the 
social  life  of  Burma.  He  received  the  marked  confidence  of 
the  Government  of  India  and  was  entrusted  with  missions 
of  a  delicate  nature.  He  was  a  scholar  of  deep  and  rare

gious and  educational  work.  Brown  University  conferred 
upon  him  the  degrees  of  Doctor  of  Divinity  and  Doctor  of
